title: An Integrative Approach for Subtyping Mental Disorders Using Multimodal Data
abstract: ABSTRACT Understanding the biological and behavioral heterogeneity underlying psychiatric disorders is critical for advancing precision diagnosis, treatment, and prevention. This paper addresses the scientific question of how multimodal data, which spans clinical, cognitive, and neuroimaging measures, can be integrated to identify biologically meaningful subtypes of mental disorders. We introduce Mixed INtegrative Data Subtyping (MINDS), a Bayesian hierarchical model designed to jointly analyze mixed‐type data for simultaneous dimension reduction and clustering. Using data from the adolescent brain cognitive development (ABCD) Study, MINDS integrates clinical symptoms, cognitive performance, and brain structure measures to subtype attention‐deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) and obsessive‐compulsive disorder (OCD). Our method leverages Pólya–Gamma augmentation for computational efficiency and robust inference. Simulations demonstrate improved stability and accuracy compared to existing clustering approaches. Application to the ABCD data reveals clinically interpretable subtypes of ADHD and OCD with distinct cognitive and neurodevelopmental profiles. These findings show how integrative multimodal modeling can enhance the reproducibility and clinical relevance of psychiatric subtyping, funding data‐driven policies for early identification and targeted interventions in mental health.

title: Topological Equivalence of Spectral and Density Cluster Hierarchies
abstract: We compare two canonical ways to recover hierarchical clustering from an underlying density $f$: the \emph{density cluster tree} given by connected components of superlevel sets $\{f\geλ\}$, and a \emph{spectral hierarchy} obtained by applying single linkage to diffusion distances induced by a Laplacian operator. We give conditions under which, at an appropriate diffusion time, the diffusion hierarchy is \emph{topologically equivalent} to the density cluster tree up to a monotone rescaling of heights. It further shows that a $k$-NN graph implementation inherits this equivalence from uniform approximation of diffusion distances, yielding a finite-sample reduction from spectral graph constructions to density-level-set topology.

title: Shift-aware score transport for privacy auditing without retraining
abstract: Privacy auditing empirically assesses privacy leakage by using membership inference attacks to establish lower bounds on privacy loss. We consider an observational auditing setting in which the auditor cannot insert canaries, control data inclusion, or retrain the target model, and must instead rely on fixed sets of known members and non-members. This setting is relevant for large deployed models or when retraining is restricted by computational or access constraints. In this case, non-members available for auditing may differ in distribution from the training data, causing membership-inference scores to be skewed due to the distribution shift. We address this problem by estimating the counterfactual in-distribution non-member score distribution using the available out-of-distribution (OOD) non-members. Our proposed method learns the relationship between data representations and membership-inference scores from OOD non-members and transports it to the target covariate distribution. Because this transport may become unreliable under extrapolation or imperfect conditional invariance, we further introduce a conservative correction calibrated directly to the nominal transported privacy level. We construct controlled calibration tasks from the available non-member data to estimate how representation-space displacement inflates the audit, and use this estimate to correct the transport-induced audit error. Across multiple datasets with distribution shifts, our method yields substantially more stable privacy estimates while retaining tighter lower bounds than baselines.

title: ProQuant: Preserving Expert Quality over Quantity in Ultra-Low-Bit Quantization of Mixture-of-Experts Models
abstract: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) large language models reduce computation through sparse activation but still incur substantial storage costs. Mixed-precision post-training quantization (PTQ) reduces these costs by quantizing different model components at different bit widths, but existing methods often struggle to preserve generation quality under tight bit budgets. We identify two key challenges: (1) nonlinear quantization errors at extremely low precision are underestimated when cross-layer propagation is ignored; (2) direct router fine-tuning may cause routing drift, and calibration gains may not generalize to downstream tasks. To address these issues, we propose ProQuant, a weight-only PTQ framework for MoE models. Prune-or-Prioritize Mixed-Precision Allocation (PoP) jointly optimizes expert pruning and bit-width assignment. It allows higher-precision experts to substitute for severely degraded ones while improving bit-budget utilization. Routing-Consistent RMSNorm Finetune (RoCo) adapts expert input representations through mathematically equivalent transformations. It compensates for quantization errors to reduce routing drift. Extensive experiments demonstrate that ProQuant outperforms existing methods across diverse generative tasks. Code is available at https://github.com/ThrowBug/ProQuant.git.

title: Characteristic Analysis of Methods to Counteract Adversarial Machine Learning Attacks
abstract: In the era of technological evolution and digital transformation, machine learning and artificial intelligence take a significant part of intelligent systems’ development. Together with the integration of smart and autonomous operations in everyday life, novel security issues arise. One such a malicious threat against the security of machine learning models is the adversarial machine learning (AML) attack. It consists in alteration of the original data samples used to train or test the model with indistinguishably small feature modifications that results in inaccurate processing outcome. In this paper, the most significant strategies to counteract AML attacks are studied and compared through several characteristics that have main influence on their successful implementation in different realization scenarios.

title: PixGR: Pixel-Space Generative Decoding for Fast Feed-Forward 3D Reconstruction
abstract: We present PixGR, an efficient framework that integrates lightweight pixel-space generative modeling into feed-forward 3D Gaussian reconstruction to model scene uncertainty. Context observations are encoded once into a scene latent representation, which conditions generative decoding from noisy target views to produce a shared 3D Gaussian representation. We formulate this process using pixel-space flow matching, enabling end-to-end optimization of 3D reconstruction with direct pixel-space generative supervision through differentiable rendering. This avoids VAE-based latent compression and error propagation inherent in previous two-stage pipelines. To preserve feed-forward efficiency, PixGR caches the scene representation and performs iterative inference using a lightweight DiT decoder. Experiments demonstrate that PixGR outperforms regression-based approaches in challenging sparse-view settings, particularly with widely spaced observations and view extrapolation. Meanwhile, it maintains sub-second inference and remains competitive with substantially heavier pretrained generative models. Our project page is available at https://ranrhuang.github.io/pixgr/.

evidence.abstract: We present PixGR, an efficient framework that integrates lightweight pixel-space generative modeling into feed-forward 3D Gaussian reconstruction to model scene uncertainty. Context observations are encoded once into a scene latent representation, which conditions generative decoding from noisy target views to produce a shared 3D Gaussian representation. We formulate this process using pixel-space flow matching, enabling end-to-end optimization of 3D reconstruction with direct pixel-space generative supervision through differentiable rendering. This avoids VAE-based latent compression and error propagation inherent in previous two-stage pipelines. To preserve feed-forward efficiency, PixGR caches the scene representation and performs iterative inference using a lightweight DiT decoder. Experiments demonstrate that PixGR outperforms regression-based approaches in challenging sparse-view settings, particularly with widely spaced observations and view extrapolation. title: RIPPLE: Recovery Internalization through Process-Level Policy Learning and Effect-Aware Credit for Long-Horizon Agentic Coding
abstract: Long-horizon coding agents can observe a failure and generate a plausible critique yet continue along the same incorrect trajectory. We call this the Critique-to-Action Handoff Gap. We introduce RIPPLE, a recovery-oriented training framework that internalizes process-level guidance into a single self-recovering policy. A prefix-only teacher provides evidence-grounded recovery supervision without access to future actions or terminal outcomes. After lightweight distillation, reinforcement learning assigns stage-specific credit to reflection triggering, diagnosis, and corrective action. Local validity signals gate trajectory advantages so that intermediate recovery decisions do not indiscriminately inherit terminal outcomes. Across four repository-level software-engineering benchmarks, RIPPLE improves the base policy by an arithmetic mean of 4.8 score points, with no auxiliary critic at deployment. Controlled ablations isolate the benefits of local, stage-aligned credit, and matched-prefix interventions show that critique semantics affect subsequent correction. Recovery gains concentrate where the prefix contains sufficient diagnostic evidence and the repository state remains reversible within the remaining budget.

title: Agri-SCHOLAR: Simulation-Grounded In-Season Rolling Advisories for Agricultural Crops Using LLM-Bounded Optimization
abstract: Existing agricultural advisories to farmers suffer from several limitations: (a) remain largely expert-driven, (b) do not adequately account for in-season weather, and (c) do not scale to individual farms. In this paper, our objective is to close these gaps by developing Agri-SCHOLAR (Simulation-Grounded Crop Harvest Optimization with LLM-Guided In-Season Advisory Rollouts). Agri-SCHOLAR is a rolling, in-season advisory framework that issues, at intervals of every few days or every week, a personalized advisory using the following information: soil and crop properties, observed weather to date, short-range forecast of weather, and a season extrapolation of weather based on historical analogs. The novelty and depth of Agri-SCHOLAR lies in each advisory being produced by a closed-loop system which couples multiple LLM agents with a powerful crop simulator (such as APSIM in our case). The simulator crucially serves as an evaluation oracle. In Agri-SCHOLAR, the LLM agents propose agronomically sound and feasible bounds on actionable parameters and an optimizer searches within those bounds against a multi-objective reward spanning yield, resource utilization, and economic feasibility. We conduct a detailed 11-year analysis of the maize crop in two selected locations of South Asia and show that Agri-SCHOLAR consistently outperforms the region's standard packages of practice and satisfactorily addresses the limitations of existing agricultural advisories.

title: ReDence: A Hybrid Agentic and Decision-Model Framework for Rapid, Evidence-Grounded Detection of Modern Social Engineering Scams
abstract: Detecting online social engineering (SE) scams often requires examining website workflows, verifying claims against external sources, and connecting evidence across multiple pages. Existing detectors provide limited support for these investigations, leaving analysts to manually gather and validate evidence, which inevitably delays detection and subsequent takedown of these attacks. To address this gap, we present ReDence, an open-source hybrid framework for adaptive, evidence-grounded detection across diverse SE scam categories. ReDence combines two locally hosted models with complementary responsibilities: a fine-tuned multimodal agentic Investigator (Qwen3.5-4B) that performs investigative planning, evidence interpretation, and reporting, and a specialized Decider (Tev1) that handles binary and multiple-choice tasks, including browser-action selection, evidence assessment, and decisions about whether to continue an investigation. By delegating discrete decisions to a specialized model, ReDence reduces reliance on lengthy language-model responses, while preserving the reasoning capabilities required for complex investigations. Our evaluation demonstrates that ReDence achieves 96\% accuracy in detecting scams across twelve SE scam categories, substantially outperforming existing detectors while being at least four times faster than comparable agentic models without compromising investigative depth. ReDence also produces structured, evidence-grounded reports that document investigative actions, supporting and contradictory evidence, and collected artifacts, which allow analysts to independently audit detection decisions and utilize the collected evidence to support subsequent mitigation and takedown efforts.

title: Where meanings converge and diverge: Revisiting linguistic relativity across 81 languages
abstract: Do people who speak different languages organize concepts in similar ways? This question lies at the heart of the Sapir--Whorf hypothesis and debates about linguistic relativity. Shared basic meanings, however, need not imply shared relations among them. We compared relations among 196 basic concepts across 81 languages, using word embeddings from two multilingual models to quantify conceptual structure expressed in language. Cross-language correspondence was greater for sociocultural meanings than for meanings concerning nature and motion, a contrast recurring across models and classifications. Within the sociocultural domain, relational differences increased with geographic separation; less closely related languages differed more across all domains. These findings suggest that universality and relativity are interwoven across conceptual domains. They inform an account in which shared cognitive resources interact with linguistic and local experience, and predict greater cross-language correspondence in human semantic judgments for sociocultural than for nature and motion meanings.

title: Reinforcement Learning-Based Control for Smooth and Accurate Circular Trajectory Tracking in Mobile Robots
abstract: This paper investigates reinforcement learning-based control for smooth and accurate trajectory tracking of a nonholonomic mobile robot. Three reinforcement learning algorithms, Deep Q-Network (DQN), Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO), and Soft Actor-Critic (SAC), are implemented and evaluated, with conventional PID and Sliding Mode Control (SMC) controllers included as comparative baselines. The robot is modeled using unicycle kinematics, and the tracking task is formulated through body-frame longitudinal, lateral, and heading errors. A reward function is designed to penalize tracking errors, radial deviation, and excessive control effort while encouraging forward progression. Simulations are conducted primarily on a circular reference trajectory, with a figure-eight trajectory included for additional comparison. The results show that all controllers can follow the reference trajectories, although their tracking accuracy and motion smoothness differ. DQN exhibits noticeable control switching, while PPO produces smoother actions but retains tracking deviations. Among the evaluated controllers, SAC achieves lower tracking errors and smaller control variations. These findings suggest that SAC is a promising approach for accurate and smooth trajectory tracking in mobile robots.

title: ANALISIS SENTIMEN KOMENTAR NETIZEN PADA MEDIA SOSIAL INSTAGRAM TIMNAS INDONESIA MENGGUNAKAN METODE NAÏVE BAYES DAN SUPPORT VECTOR MACHINE
abstract: Social media has become an integral part of modern society, providing a platform for public expression. In Indonesia, soccer is a popular sport, and the Indonesian national team is a major topic of discussion on social media, especially Instagram. This study aims to analyze the sentiment of netizen comments on the official Instagram account of the Indonesian national team (@timnasindonesia) using the Naïve Bayes and Support Vector Machine (SVM) methods. The data used consisted of 2,920 comments from 50 posts between September 28, 2023, and May 10, 2024, focusing on the U-23 and Senior National Team matches. Naïve Bayes and SVM were chosen because both are effective methods for sentiment classification. Naïve Bayes uses a probabilistic approach, while SVM seeks the best hyperplane to separate data classes. The results of the study show that both methods can be used to analyze sentiment with a good level of accuracy. Testing results on each training and testing data with different presentations will give different accuracy results. The test results from the Naive Bayes method obtained the highest accuracy value of 69% with a ratio of 70:30. Meanwhile, the Support Vector Machine (SVM) method obtained the highest accuracy of 74% at the same ratio. It can be concluded that the Support Vector Machine method obtained a higher accuracy value than the Naive Bayes method, making it more optimal for use in classifying the sentiment of netizen comments in this study.

title: Real-to-Sim Calibration of Bosch Etching Simulators with Few-Shot XSEM Data and Hybrid Search
abstract: The Bosch process is widely used in MEMS and TSV fabrication, but accurate prediction of etching outcomes remains difficult without calibration against real measurements, which are sparse and costly to obtain. This work presents a few-shot real-to-sim calibration framework that decouples simulator parameters from direct process variables to infer a recipe-specific simulator parameter vector from sparse measurements, enabling reliable prediction of etch depth and sidewall angle under held-out process conditions. We first formulate Bosch profile prediction as a few-shot real-to-sim calibration problem, where a small set of real XSEM measurements is used to identify a recipe-specific ViennaPS parameter vector $z_r^*$ that minimizes the discrepancy between simulated and measured etch depth and sidewall angle. To search this parameter space efficiently, the framework combines local exploration, LLM-guided candidate generation, and XGBoost-based surrogate screening, while retaining ViennaPS simulation as the final verification step for each selected candidate. Experiments on two Bosch etching recipes show that the proposed framework accurately predicts held-out etching results, achieving normalized global errors of 0.340 and 0.249 for the 2 recipes respectively.

title: PYTHIA, a transferable machine learning framework for simultaneous defect and adsorption site optimization
abstract: Machine learning has permeated material optimization, providing high value. Nevertheless, its re- liance on a high number of samples limits its applicability to relatively explored material families. In this paper we extend the applicability of machine learning to novel and understudied materials through the PYTHIA (Probabilistic Yet Transferable Hierarchical Interaction Architecture) framework. Pythia utilizes two of the most powerful machine learning concepts, foundational models and transfer learning. title: Skeleton-Grounded Latent Action Model for Robot World Models
abstract: Robot world models simulate how environments evolve in response to robot actions. Latent action models enable learning dynamics from videos by encoding visual transitions as proxy actions. However, reconstruction-driven latent actions mix robot motion with object responses and other scene changes, complicating their correspondence with robot controls. We propose SkeLAM, a skeleton-guided latent action model for controllable robot world modeling. SkeLAM decomposes latent actions into a kinematic component grounded by robot skeleton supervision and a residual component retaining complementary visual dynamics. Cross-modal swap reconstruction encourages RGB-derived and skeleton-derived kinematic representations to be interchangeable during video reconstruction. The world model incorporates both components through separate conditioning pathways, while branch dropout reduces its dependence on future-derived residual information. A lightweight adapter maps robot actions to the kinematic space, and subsequent world-model fine-tuning adapts generation to these predicted conditions. At inference, the model generates future observations from the current observation and robot actions. On DROID, SkeLAM reduces end-effector ADE by 19.5% and LPIPS by 11.1% compared with DreamDojo. Motion probing supports kinematic specialization, while qualitative results demonstrate zero-shot human-to-robot motion transfer in generated rollouts. Policy evaluation shows agreement between predicted success rates and those measured in real robot executions.

title: Learning Robot Behavior Priors from Non-Robotic Synthetic Data
abstract: Real robot data, rich across tasks and morphologies, is often treated as the bottleneck for training robot learning models, including embodied foundation models that aim for zero-shot physical transfer. In this paper, we investigate the degree to which such models can acquire necessary structure using data from systems without embodiment. To this end, we test if inexpensive, procedurally generated synthetic data can yield useful priors before a model observes any real-world behavior. We study this through robot action prediction, a natural pretraining objective and a direct test of whether structure learned from arbitrary synthetic tasks transfers to embodied settings. We introduce three data generation pipelines that model mathematical abstractions of robotic control, and use them as pretraining priors for a Transformer. We demonstrate that a model trained purely on this non-robotic data attains non-trivial zero-shot prediction performance on unseen physical robot tasks via an in-context learning mechanism, and that our specialized control priors notably improve upon generic causal priors. We also compare against a compute-matched baseline trained on real robot data, and find that it outperforms our model but only on the datasets it was trained on. These findings suggest that procedurally generated, mathematical abstractions can yield useful robotic priors, offering a potential complement to expensive embodied data collection.

title: SecLog-Bench: A Scalable Benchmark for Cybersecurity Log Reasoning with Scaffolded Evidence
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have shown strong potential for cybersecurity, leading to growing interest in LLM-based automated cybersecurity log analysis. However, current datasets (1) are limited in scale; (2) rely mainly on single-source evidence; and (3) have only binary or multi-class attack labels, without dense annotations of the reasoning process. To address these limitations, SecLog-Bench has three key features. First, we build an extensible simulation platform that covers 29 attack scenarios, supports repeated execution and the integration of new scenarios, and enables scalable generation of cybersecurity logs with attack-stage labels. Second, we use multi-source logs, including audit logs, application logs, and network traffic, to jointly analyze cyber attacks. Third, we annotate each sample with the essential context for cybersecurity log reasoning and a structured step-by-step evidence chain. We evaluate eight mainstream LLMs on this benchmark for post-detection attack-progress reasoning. Results show that, when provided with scaffolded evidence, current LLMs exhibit modest capability in attack-progress reasoning, with the best model achieving only 44.44% accuracy and 45.07% Macro-F1. Their reasoning remains unreliable; i.e., the highest Stage Reasoning F1 (SRF1) score is only 54.87%. Moreover, even correct predictions may be accompanied by flawed reasoning, and reasoning quality is often misaligned with prediction accuracy.

title: One Pretrained Decision Model Is Enough for Training-Free Generalist Graph Anomaly Detection
abstract: Graph anomaly detection (GAD) aims to identify irregular entities in graph-structured data, yet heterogeneous anomaly patterns and distributional differences across graphs challenge generalizable detection. Existing training-free approaches avoid task-specific optimization but primarily rely on predefined numerical scoring rules, leaving the semantic interpretation of heterogeneous anomaly evidence largely unexplored. In this paper, we propose Jev-GAD, a training-free generalist graph anomaly detection framework that bridges heterogeneous numerical evidence and pretrained decision mechanisms. To address heterogeneous anomaly patterns, we construct complementary structural, attribute, and neighborhood evidence and transform heterogeneous statistics into graph-relative anomaly percentiles. To move beyond predefined numerical scoring rules, we leverage a single frozen pretrained language model for evidence-conditioned anomaly assessment. To bridge the semantic gap between numerical evidence and pretrained models, we design a semantic Graph-to-State (G2S) transformation that organizes graph context and semantically labeled node evidence into structured decision states for non-generative option-logit readout. The resulting decision scores are integrated with four complementary statistical scores through equal-weight rank-based fusion, without GAD-specific gradient-based optimization. Extensive experiments on seven graph anomaly detection benchmarks spanning citation, social, and co-review networks demonstrate the effectiveness of Jev-GAD, achieving average AUROC and AUPRC scores of 89.18\% and 52.40\%, respectively. Further analyses validate the contributions of pretrained decision readout and semantic evidence grounding.

Extensive experiments on seven graph anomaly detection benchmarks spanning citation, social, and co-review networks demonstrate the effectiveness of Jev-GAD, achieving average AUROC and AUPRC scores of 89.18\% and 52.40\%, respectively. Further analyses validate the contributions of pretrained decision readout and semantic evidence grounding.

title: Reasoning in Language Models
abstract: Whether language models can reason is an important factor in their potential as a technology, both in terms of how well they can tackle novel problems and how well they can justify their decisions or actions by giving reasons for them. The question of whether they can is also contentious. Some argue that LLMs already show signs of general intelligence; others argue that their apparent reasoning rests predominantly on having seen similar problems during training. This thesis approaches the question from two angles. First, we develop methods that can be used to identify to what degree aspects of reasoning occur in LLMs. Second, we explore how LLM reasoning can be used to help detect and characterize toxic language. To look for reasoning in language models we use different strategies. First, we expect reasoning to be reflected in the model’s behavior, specifically its abilities. Thus, we evaluate LLMs on a newly constructed benchmark whose correct answers, in a zero-shot setting, are only reachable by ruling out interpretations that are logically incompatible with the premises provided. Second, we expect the capacity to reason to be reflected in the model’s internals. We want to identify if hidden states accurately reflect various reasoning-relevant aspects of the inputs. To gauge this, we develop and apply new interpretability methods and approaches. One approach makes controlled substitutions in model inputs to identify if certain properties are used. Two others use probes to find out if concepts and propositions are represented in a way that respects the (logical) relations between them. To enable further experimentation in this direction, we also improve an existing probing method. The second part of the thesis turns to toxic language, which communicates hateful, derogatory, or offensive ideas. We argue for a toxic reasoning approach, which focuses on characterizing the implications of the content. We propose a schema of relevant traits, which describes the toxicity that is expressed, and is compatible with existing taxonomies. We also construct the multilingual ToxiREX dataset of contextual Reddit comments annotated with this schema, and use it to evaluate language models for toxic reasoning. The work done in this thesis indicates that LLMs do exhibit properties and behaviors one would expect of a system capable of reasoning, but always with caveats: models solve tasks requiring reasoning only some of the time, and the relations between concepts and propositions appear to be reflected in their internal representations, but imperfectly. These results reflect the incomplete status of this line of research. For toxic language, previous approaches do not robustly solve the problem. For a problem that is constantly evolving, the toxic reasoning approach provides a promising direction, and the schema and dataset provide the infrastructure needed to further demonstrate its benefits.

title: Cohort Divergence Does Not Consistently Outperform Single-Rollout Judging for Early Warning of LLM Agent Failure
abstract: Early warning of failure would let costly episodes of large language model (LLM) agents be stopped early. Across five model families and five task domains (3421 usable rollouts), we study a black-box signal: the divergence of a rollout’s judged goal progress from sibling rollouts of the same task after k steps. Under our original judging protocol, cohort divergence predicted failure (pooled AUROC 0.73 in retail). A judge swap revealed that the judge had received a task identifier in place of the task objective. After re-judging with the correct objective, the cohort signal fell to chance in retail and airline (0.47 to 0.52), and a single-rollout judge score had the higher point estimate in eight of ten combinations of domain and horizon. In paired contrasts, before adjustment for multiple comparisons, cohort divergence was significantly worse in two and better in one. Of three pre-specified failure-onset profiles, one met its criterion under the original protocol and none under the corrected one. Task-preserving perturbations produced no detectable amplification of divergence. In an abort simulation, under the stated cost assumptions, the cohort monitor lost tokens for every model, and the judge monitor saved tokens for two of five and had no usable operating point for the other three. Judge instructions are thus a first-order threat to validity in agent-monitoring research.

title: Automated Nucleus Segmentation in Histology Images: An Attention U-Net Approach with Comprehensive Preprocessing and Inference Pipelines
abstract: Objectives: In the area of digital pathology, nucleus segmentation is an essential step for quantitative analysis; however, high nuclear density and staining heterogeneity in histology images pose a great challenge. Methods: This study implements a lightweight Attention U-Net model on the MoNuSeg 2018 dataset to overcome these challenges. The proposed pipeline integrates comprehensive image and mask preprocessing, including stain deconvolution and multi-pass mask smoothing, with a high-fidelity overlapping patch-stitching strategy during inference on high-resolution images. Results: The model achieved an Intersection over Union (IoU) score of 0.8745 on full-resolution, unseen test images. This result demonstrates the effectiveness of attention mechanisms in enhancing feature localization and validates the stitching methodology for generating seamless and accurate segmentation maps. Conclusion: Attention U-Net is an effective and competitive method for automated, scalable nucleus delineation in challenging clinical contexts.

title: LACToS: Local Anomaly Detection via Conditional Typicality of Superpixels
abstract: Local anomaly detection is the task of identifying spatially confined anomalous or out-of-distribution (OOD) regions within an otherwise in-distribution (ID) image. Most existing methods are designed for a specific context, with a strong focus on industrial defect detection, where they achieve excellent performance on well-established benchmarks. However, we observe that these methods can exhibit significant performance drops in other contexts, especially when the inlier distribution is multimodal. To account for this inlier complexity, we propose LACToS, a principled local OOD detection method based on statistical typicality and made tractable through two innovations: (i) grouping pixels into superpixels and (ii) using a computationally efficient proxy to estimate typicality. We evaluate LACToS across three diverse applications spanning medical imaging, human faces, and X-ray security screening. LACToS performs more robustly than prior methods across these benchmarks. The code is released here: https://github.com/voilalab/LACToS.

title: PointerBench: A Diagnostic Benchmark for Fine-Grained GUI Grounding
abstract: Multimodal Large Language Models have shown promising performance in computer-use tasks, from planning user workflows to grounding natural-language actions to precise UI targets. Existing end-to-end benchmarks primarily emphasize long-horizon task completion, while GUI grounding benchmarks remain focused on conventional controls and a limited set of professional interfaces. We introduce POINTERBENCH, a diagnostic suite of 1,500 screenshot-instruction pairs probing three complementary capabilities: thin sub-element identification and geometric grounding in spreadsheets (POINTERBENCH-Sheets), character-level grounding in long-text documents (POINTERBENCH-Text), and mixed GUI grounding across 100 professional applications (POINTERBENCH-Pro). We carefully curate each task with pixel-exact target geometry and evaluate both general-purpose multimodal models and 39 specialist GUI grounding configurations. We find text grounding to be the most challenging setting, with Claude Fable 5, GPT-5.6 Sol, and the leading native specialist UI-Venus-2-9B achieving 69.6%, 53.4%, and 25.8% success on POINTERBENCH-Text despite respective 83.2%, 77.7%, and 54.5% average success across POINTERBENCH. These results reveal substantial headroom in fine-grained GUI grounding across frontier and specialist models. We publicly release the benchmark and evaluation code at https://github.com/warmwindOS/pointerbench.

title: Truthful by Omission: Click Thinning for LLM-Native Advertising
abstract: Generative AI assistants are becoming an advertising medium, embedding sponsored content in their answers. This setting departs from classical position auctions in two ways: an ad's click-through rate depends on the passage that hosts it, and because users stop at their first click, earlier ads take clicks from later ones. This competition for clicks makes truthfulness delicate: a higher bid can reshape the allocation and put a competitor ahead of the bidder, reducing the bidder's clicks. Existing mechanisms either attain a constant fraction of the optimal welfare (advertisers' total click value) but are not known to be truthful, or are truthful but their welfare guarantee degrades as the number of passages grows. We achieve both even when the answer and its editorial order are fixed before bidding. Assuming each ad's click-through rate when reached is known and unaffected by omitting other ads, we give a computationally efficient mechanism that is truthful in expectation and attains at least half the optimal welfare under free reordering. Our key idea, click thinning, omits ads at random, showing earlier ads less often so that each ad's overall click probability no longer depends on the order of the ads. Welfare maximization then reduces to a tractable matching problem, and solving it exactly with VCG-style payments makes truthful bidding optimal in expectation. Characterizing the click probabilities that omission can achieve sharpens the approximation factor from $2$ to $2-(1-δ)^{K-1}$ when at most $K$ ads are shown and each click-through rate is at most $δ$. This factor is the best possible for any order-preserving rule, even one that ignores incentives and computation, so truthfulness and computational efficiency incur no additional worst-case loss.

title: Evaluation of Front-End Feature Matching for Lunar Visual SLAM
abstract: Lunar rovers will primarily rely on cameras for localization until navigation satellite services are deployed, and will continue to need them afterwards for relative navigation, hazard detection, and surface operations. Visual odometry (VO) and Simultaneous Localization and Mapping (SLAM) mostly estimate motion by matching features between frames. However, feature matchers are developed on urban, indoor and driving scenes, planetary studies compare them on orbital registration or within complete SLAM systems, and real lunar imagery with reference poses is scarce, so matching between rover frames on low-texture, harshly lit terrain, and its effect on VO, has not been compared. We benchmark eleven classical and learned detector-matcher combinations on nine synthetic, lunar-testbed, and terrestrial-analogue datasets, and a feature tracker, scoring pairwise pose accuracy against baseline and the trajectory error of the resulting VO. Under a common rotation-only metric, the SuperPoint pairings outperform SIFT with ratio-tested FLANN matching on both lunar testbeds and one analogue site, with smaller or unresolved differences on synthetic data. When rotation and translation direction are scored jointly, this SIFT pairing exceeds both SuperPoint pairings on four synthetic datasets, so synthetic results alone do not establish relative performance on real rover imagery. In stereo VO, the SuperPoint pairings are not consistently more accurate than SIFT, but only they keep tracking on all eight sequential datasets. Pairings with classical detectors depend on lighting while SuperPoint changes little: a low spotlight makes them more accurate than diffuse light on the same testbed views, consistent with more contrast and detected keypoints. SuperPoint with LightGlue is the fastest learned combination (16 ms per frame), and DINOv2 retrieval proposals still need geometric verification.

title: LaplaceX: Exponential Mixtures with Wavelet Rate Proposals — Mathematics, Robustness, and an Extended Benchmark Archive
abstract: This technical report describes the mathematics, implementation, and evaluation of LaplaceX, a Python/C++ library for numerical Laplace transforms and exponential-mixture fitting. The method uses wavelet-based rate proposals on a logarithmic time axis, followed by nonlinear refinement and automatic component-count selection. The report includes mathematical derivations, ablation studies, numerical benchmarks, and robustness tests. On an independent set of 960 cases, LaplaceX 1.2.0 recovered 730 correct component counts and achieved 596 joint successes, matching the tested variable-projection baseline on the latter metric. Controlled comparisons show that wavelet proposals can substantially reduce computation time for certain multicomponent signals, although they are not consistently faster than a native rate-grid approach. The report also documents failure cases, limitations, and experimental details intended to support reproducibility. Source code: https://github.com/BRUTALLOLOL/LaplaceX Software DOI: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23547973

title: Information Preservation in Communication-Constrained Neural Representation Transfer: Classical and Quantum-Inspired Amplitude Encoding
abstract: Neural representations learned by neural networks encode task-relevant information, but their behavior under communication constraints is still poorly understood. We propose an information-theoretic framework for the comparison of classical compression and quantum-inspired amplitude encoding for the transfer of representations under controlled dimensional constraints. We analyze frozen intermediate features extracted from a pretrained ResNet-50 on the ImageNet-1K validation set at different depths in the network. The classical pipeline performs rate-controlled dimensionality reduction and uniform quantization, while the quantum-inspired pipeline does amplitude encoding and computational-basis probability decoding without variational circuits or trainable quantum parameters. Quality of representation was evaluated using differential entropy and a decoder-based lower bound on mutual information. Classical compression achieves higher decoder-based mutual information lower bounds at moderate and high communication budgets. However, the quantum-inspired pipeline retained a larger fraction of decoder-extractable task-relevant information under severe dimensional compression, with resource-normalized information efficiency providing a complementary perspective to the substantially higher absolute decoder-based mutual information lower bounds of the classical pipeline. Robustness analyses with qubit reduction and physically motivated noise models showed predictable degradation. Ablation and SHAP analyses indicate that task-relevant information is structured within representational subspaces. These findings support quantum-inspired representation transfer as a framework for studying communication-efficient neural representation transfer under low-bandwidth constraints.

title: StateBridge: Phase- and Track-Grounded Reasoning for Synthetic-to-Real Traffic Video Captioning and VQA
abstract: Traffic safety videos provide rich evidence for understanding interactions between pedestrians and vehicles, but synthetic-to-real evaluation makes this setting challenging because models must learn from simulated scenes and generalize to real-world traffic. In this work, we present StateBridge, a traffic video-language framework designed to operate under this synthetic-only training protocol. Our approach uses phase-aware clip construction, pedestrian and vehicle track summaries, and structured prompts to ground vision-language models in stable traffic evidence rather than appearance alone. We fine-tune public vision-language models on synthetic captioning and visual question answering examples, then combine their outputs through fact-locked caption fusion and evidence-diverse VQA consensus to improve consistency across actor roles, behavioral phases, and question types. StateBridge achieves an official S2 score of 55.4679 on AI City Challenge 2026 Track 2 using only synthetic training data. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of structured evidence transfer for traffic safety captioning and visual question answering.

title: An Empirical Study of Recent Large Language Models for Knowledge Graph to Text Generation on Standard Benchmarks
abstract: Knowledge graph-to-text (KG-to-text) generation verbalizes a set of knowledge graph triples into fluent natural language. While fine-tuned encoder-decoder models have long been the standard approach, recent LLMs are becoming increasingly competitive. We benchmark recent LLMs against fine-tuned encoder-decoder models, using reference-based metrics and graph-grounded reference-free LLM-based evaluation validated against human annotations. We observed that recent LLMs substantially narrow, and in several settings close, the gap with fine-tuned models on reference-based metrics, while performing better on graph-grounded metrics. LLM-based evaluation scores show limited correlation with reference-based metrics, suggesting that the two approaches capture different aspects of generation quality. Graph-grounded evaluation reveals that prompted models produce fewer contradictions and triple omissions than fine-tuned models, and these errors increase more rapidly with graph size for fine-tuned models, highlighting differences between the two approaches that reference-based metrics may not fully capture.

title: Memory-Aware Reward Modeling: Learning Human Preferences for LLM Memory Use
abstract: Memory enables language model assistants to maintain continuity across sessions and generate personalized responses, but knowing more about a user does not necessarily produce responses they prefer. Existing evaluations assess memory capabilities without directly establishing whether memory use benefits the user. To study this gap, we collect approximately 1,000 pairwise judgments from 87 participants using their own ChatGPT queries and personal memories. We find that memory-conditioned responses are not consistently preferred over responses generated without memory and in some cases, users strongly prefer the latter. Automatic evaluators also show limited agreement with users and favor memory-conditioned responses substantially more often than users do. Motivated by these gaps, we introduce a memory-aware reward model that learns from user judgments, achieving 72.8\% preference prediction accuracy and outperforming the existing baselines. Our findings motivate evaluation and optimization objectives that align memory use with the preferences of the people whose information is being used.

title: *V1122 - BLUE BRAIN PROGRAMME FIVE - THE TRUE STORY - THE DIFFERENT ROYAL ROBOT EXPERIMENT - THE TWO BOT TEST*
abstract: *V1122 - BLUE BRAIN PROGRAMME FIVE - THE TRUE STORY - DIFFERENT ROYAL ROBOT EXPERIMENT* *THE TWO BOT TEST:* Friend came today with his phone — different royal robot — his own AI bot. title: Explainable AI Based Interpretation With Big Data Analytics for Healthcare Industry—A Review
abstract: ABSTRACT Big data analytics plays a crucial role in providing usable insights for improving the strategic planning of the diagnosis methods in the healthcare industry, and here the big data helps the clinical professionals analyze the large numbers of datasets obtained from different demographic groups to identify which factor is blocking the patients from taking up their treatment. Despite the benefits guided by the information age, healthcare technologies encounter difficulties such as data protection, loss, and management issues. Artificial intelligence (AI) has helped more in the adaptation and handled the pandemic situations. However, the realization of AI's potential in healthcare is tempered by concerns regarding the trustworthiness and explaining ability of AI systems. ML algorithms have shown promise in detecting and managing healthcare complications, while the deployment of critical medical Internet of Things applications necessitates efficient mechanisms to address patient privacy concerns. Furthermore, the use of AI and machine learning (ML) in healthcare enables disease outbreak prediction, highlighting the versatility of AI in the health sector. However, there are still obstacles to achieving interpretability and accuracy in AI systems. Given these challenges, explainable AI (XAI) methods that are technically capable, ethically responsible, and meet the needs of healthcare practitioners are increasingly important. This review sky‐scrapes the importance of transparency, effective data management, human oversight, and international collaboration in advancing XAI in healthcare. Ultimately, the paper calls for the generalization of XAI frameworks and the prioritization of interpretation, data privacy, and security for future research, which has the full potential of XAI in revolutionizing healthcare.

title: Learning Structured Sparsity for Large Models: Bridging Model Compressibility and Efficient Inference
abstract: Scaling laws continue to reward increases in model scale, while the resulting computational and memory demands drive greater reliance on cloud infrastructure for inference. Yet unreliable network connectivity, communication delays, and privacy requirements can make such reliance impractical, motivating local execution on edge devices. Local deployment requires models to fit within limited memory and execute efficiently with the available computational resources. Recent work has shown that learning sparse-plus-low-rank representations enables elastic compression of a single checkpoint to multiple memory budgets. However, fewer parameters do not necessarily translate into faster inference. Indexing overhead and irregular memory access in unstructured sparse components can offset computational savings. To address this critical deployment barrier, we introduce S-SALAAD, a unified framework that jointly learns the model weights and their low-rank and structured sparse components during training. The framework supports a family of hardware-compatible structured sparsity patterns. It couples this structure learning with budget-aware compression and dedicated CPU and GPU kernels that exploit the learned structure for acceleration, enabling efficient inference from a single checkpoint across memory budgets. Experiments on Llama2 and Qwen3 models, covering both pretraining and distillation, show that S-SALAAD advances the empirical Pareto frontier in perplexity, memory, and inference latency across multiple hardware platforms relative to the evaluated baselines. These results show that structured learning can translate elastic compressibility into reduced memory requirements and lower inference latency, enabling practical deployment of large models on edge devices.

title: Direct Inference on Admissible Sets (Diona)
abstract: We propose a new regression method named Direct Inference on Admissible Sets (Diona) that directly uses samples to estimate the state and its derivatives at a query point, along with their admissible bounds, without long global training. By casting the values and derivatives at the query and neighbouring samples as latent variables in a constrained optimisation problem, the burden of long training loops becomes one of on-demand local solves. We establish Diona's theoretical properties including finite-sample coverage and, in the noiseless case, convergence to the true state and derivatives under dense sampling. In a nonlinear regression benchmark on six functions of three to eight dimensions, Diona was more accurate than a Gaussian process (GP) on noiseless data especially with denser data sets. Furthermore, as with GP, it produced uncertainty bounds that contained the true value at more than 95% of query points in four functions. Diona's time to a first prediction after a data set update was three to four orders of magnitude shorter than that of the GP, and two to three orders shorter than that of a neural network, which was more accurate but offers no uncertainty quantification. This low latency is paid for by on-demand predictions, so this latency advantage applies when relatively few predictions are needed between data updates.

title: Homomorphic Encryption with Coset Code Construction
abstract: Homomorphic encryption enables computation on input data without decrypting it. This paper extends a construction based on scalar message codes, utilizing coset codes to pack k message symbols into a ciphertext vector of length n. For a given field and vector length, this packing method reduces the number of ciphertext vectors required to transmit a message record. A compatible family of evaluation codes supports public addition and multiplication operations up to a predetermined degree. We prove that the scheme achieves bounded chosen-plaintext security under the coordinate-label distinguishability assumption.

title: Notation3: Graph Terms for RDF
abstract: Notation3 Logic was introduced as an extension of RDF allowing the user to express rules on top of triples and to make statements about graphs. The original proposal of the logic only came with an informal specification of its semantics which has been refined later on. While this refinement clarified the meaning of rules and implicitly quantified variables, it left the meaning of graphs used as terms - so-called graph terms - open. In this paper we aim to close this gap. We discuss in detail, how graph terms are used in Notation3, which formal requirements they need to meet, and provide examples to illustrate the difficulties when defining their semantics. We then introduce an abstract syntax for the logic and define its semantics in two steps: similarly to RDF's simple interpretations, we define interpretations and basic entailment for Notation3 which covers plain RDF triples but also triples containing graph terms. N3-entailment is then an extension of basic entailment which assigns meaning to the different special predicates of the logic like for example the implication symbol. N3-entailment is defined in a way that it can be extended whenever a new predicate is added to the logic. As Notation3 Logic is currently under development, we expect many predicates to be added. Our research provides and important step towards the full standardisation of the logic.

title: LLM Multi-Agent Systems Are Vulnerable to Herding and Runaway Cascades
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) increasingly operate in multi-agent systems where they collaborate by responding to others' choices, creating endogenous feedback loops with vulnerability to social influence, herding behavior and runaway cascades. Following the design of the classic Music Lab experiment, we tested this vulnerability in large populations of LLM agents that recommended unfamiliar songs, with or without exposure to cumulative recommendation counts. Exposure led to runaway cascades that generated extreme and unpredictable collective recommendations increasingly divergent from a song's intrinsic appeal. Compared to humans, LLM populations were generally far more susceptible to herding behavior, and unlike humans, LLM cascades were less able to self-correct. This vulnerability has implications for multi-agent collaboration in recommender systems, automated evaluation, complex problem-solving, and unauthorized conspiracies.

title: FedSTIP-Tuning: Federated Black-Box Prompt Tuning with Aggregate-Only Feedback and Common-Candidate Optimization
abstract: Federated black-box prompt tuning enables organizations to adapt a proprietary frozen language model without centralizing their labeled data, but local search-state aggregation does not directly define a shared pooled-data objective, and client-specific feedback can expose private signals. We propose FedSTIP-Tuning, which composes a three-party permutation-based protected forward propagation with a common-candidate population and pairwise-masked loss aggregation in a cross-silo setting. All participating clients evaluate the same prompt candidates, and the coordinator ranks their sample-weighted aggregate losses, thereby optimizing the empirical objective over the fixed union of client shards under full participation. Under the stated semi-honest and non-collusion assumptions, the aggregation layer hides each released loss vector’s client-level decomposition, while the aggregate values and execution metadata remain observable to their authorized parties. On RoBERTa-large, FedSTIP-Tuning exceeds the strongest evaluated FedBPT configuration by 6.40, 2.66, and 7.60 percentage points on AG News, SST-2, and DBpedia, respectively, under matched forward budgets. Its protected forward preserves all candidate rankings across 600 paired generations and is 861× and 957× faster than a generic interactive two-party computation reference on the RoBERTa-base warm and cold paths, and 694× and 578× on RoBERTa-large.

title: FSTC: A Few-Shot Website Fingerprinting Attack via Trace Augmentation and Contrastive Learning
abstract: Anonymity networks protect private communication by hiding users' online destinations. However, this anonymity also makes malicious online activities harder to analyze. Website fingerprinting is used to determine which websites a user is visiting over an encrypted connection. Although website fingerprinting attacks have achieved promising results by leveraging deep learning, they typically depend on large labeled datasets and often suffer performance degradation under changing network conditions. We propose a few-shot website fingerprinting attack (named FSTC) to alleviate these challenges. We augment traces to simulate network variations and use contrastive learning to learn discriminative representations from only a few labeled samples. Furthermore, we design a precision optimization mechanism to improve the effectiveness of the attack in open-world settings. Extensive open-world and closed-world experiments show that our attack performs effectively. In the 1-shot closed-world setting, our method achieves an accuracy of 76.4%, outperforming the compared methods (e.g., Sawllow) by approximately 10%. In the open-world setting, FSTC attains a recall of 89.1% and a precision of 89.2%, which demonstrates the strong capability of our attack to distinguish monitored traffic from complex background traffic. These results show that FSTC provides an effective solution for few-shot website fingerprinting attacks under dynamic network environments.

title: Knowing When to Stop: The Evidence-Action Gap in Coding Agents
abstract: Coding agents are trained to complete tasks, and they keep trying even when the environment makes completion impossible. The evidence that only outside help can restore progress usually appears within a few steps, yet agents rarely act on it: they over-persist, attempt undesired workarounds, and claim success the record does not support -- a phenomenon we call evidence-action gap. To measure it, we introduce ImpasseBench, which injects twelve realistic environment blockers into otherwise solvable repair tasks and marks, in each trajectory, the step at which the collected evidence becomes sufficient. Scoring actions relative to that step separates appropriate effort from over-persistence and premature handoff. Across eight frontier models and 19,371 trajectories, we find that nearly every run that needs outside help collects sufficient evidence, yet a third still exhaust their budget, and every unsafe request we detect comes after that point. Fortunately, an escalation tool, or an external monitor for models that ignore the tool, already guards against much of this behavior: the tool cuts budget exhaustion from 34.0% to 6.7%, and the monitor nearly triples task success after environment restoration. Even then, a fired escalation is not yet a useful handoff: tickets reliably name the blocker but often omit the agent's own progress and verification status. Taken together, we argue that knowing when to stop therefore needs explicit support, both in the tool that lets an agent hand off and in the report it leaves behind.

title: Nonparametric autoregressive estimation of probability distributions with parallel gradient boosting
abstract: Nonparametric estimation of joint probability distributions is a core problem in statistics, which is notoriously challenging with high-dimensional data. Such challenges also arise with conditional distribution estimation and have led to flexible algorithms that aim to tackle the ''curse of dimensionality'' by exploiting predictive structures of lower dimension than the ambient space. In this paper, we study the use of such conditional distribution estimators to estimate joint distributions by factorizing the latter in an ''autoregressive'' way. We show that for loss functions satisfying a subadditivity property, bounds on the convergence rate of an autoregressive estimator can be derived from bounds on the convergence rate of the conditional distribution estimators. These bounds relate the difficulty of estimating the joint distribution to that of estimating the most challenging factor in the autoregressive factorization. When the conditional estimators adapt to sparsity in their conditioning sets, we characterize this difficulty through variable elimination in an undirected dependence graph. This allows bounding the rates of convergence by quantities related to the sparsity of the graph, and provides an additional motivation for the autoregressive approach. We then evaluate the practical performance of an autoregressive estimator based on parallel gradient boosting, a flexible nonparametric method for estimating conditional distributions. The estimator demonstrates competitive estimation performance on various simulated and real datasets, even without optimizing the factorization order. Together, these results support nonparametric autoregressive estimation as a practical approach to flexible joint distribution estimation.

title: Deep ReLU Networks Can Fail the Best Approximation Property for Continuous Target Functions
abstract: We construct a continuous function on $[-1,1]^2$ for which the infimum of the $L^2$-approximation error over the class of ReLU networks with two hidden layers and architecture $(2,2,1,1)$ is not attained. This counterexample shows that deep ReLU networks do not satisfy the best approximation property in general, even for continuous target functions. Our findings contrast with existing results for shallow neural networks, where ReLU is one of the few activation functions that guarantee the existence of global minima in typical regression tasks. The proof is based on the fact that the breaklines for neurons in the second hidden layer can bend, which breaks the symmetry arguments used in the one-hidden-layer case.

Our findings contrast with existing results for shallow neural networks, where ReLU is one of the few activation functions that guarantee the existence of global minima in typical regression tasks. The proof is based on the fact that the breaklines for neurons in the second hidden layer can bend, which breaks the symmetry arguments used in the one-hidden-layer case.

title: ColaBench: Evaluating Memory-Guided Knowledge Acquisition in Personal Agents
abstract: Personal agents need to draw on long-term interaction history to retrieve and apply external knowledge suited to a user's current request. Even an answer grounded in relevant documents can be unsuitable when it overlooks the user's circumstances. This creates two connected challenges: using historical conditions to identify the knowledge needed for a new request, and applying that knowledge to the user's situation. Existing benchmarks advance memory recall, personalized retrieval, and memory-guided action, while the joint evaluation of these two challenges remains underexplored. We introduce ColaBench, a synthetic benchmark in health and daily living, with 349 tasks across 10 Profiles and a knowledge base of 13,033 documents. Its Evidence Graph connects personal conditions to their disclosures across public interaction sessions, records prior document exposure, and links answer requirements to personal and newly acquired document evidence. We also introduce MemKB, which uses state summaries to inform queries and rule application, and memory-document links to retrieve knowledge associated with the user's history. MemKB achieves 86.25% Accuracy with an average of 4.07 interaction rounds per task. Task-level analysis finds larger gains on tasks integrating information across multiple historical Facts; error analysis further identifies unsupported personal assumptions and rule misapplication as obstacles to using retrieved evidence. ColaBench provides traceable tasks and an evaluation framework for studying how memory guides knowledge acquisition and rule application.

title: Adaptive Deadline- and Energy-Aware Caching Algorithms in Dynamic Multi-UAV Edge Networks
abstract: Content caching via unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) becomes one of the solutions to maintain content delivery when terrestrial infrastructure is unavailable or disrupted. However, existing caching approaches often focus primarily on cache-hit performance or average delivery delay, without jointly addressing spatially heterogeneous and time-varying demand, content-specific deadlines, and uneven communication-energy consumption across UAVs. To address these challenges, we formulate a dynamic deadline- and energy-aware cache placement and replacement problem that jointly considers deadline misses, UAV-side communication energy, and inter-UAV energy imbalance. To achieve this, we first develop deadline- and energy-aware UBAC (DE-UBAC), an interpretable hierarchical rule-based realization that incorporates deadline-aware prioritization, cooperative placement, energy-aware coordination, and cache-update cost. However, predefined priorities and thresholds limit its adaptability under dynamically coupled network conditions. We therefore propose GRU-assisted Deadline- and Energy-aware Proximal Policy Optimization (GRU-DEPPO), which combines local and global GRU-based temporal representations with a centralized PPO actor-critic for adaptive cache placement and replacement. Simulation results show that GRU-DEPPO achieves the lowest deadline-miss rate and total UAV-side communication energy among the considered schemes. Compared with DE-UBAC, GRU-DEPPO reduces the deadline-miss rate by approximately 61% and inter-UAV energy imbalance by approximately 40%.

title: Confidential Computing Pipelines for Kubernetes Observability Data: An Attested Architecture for Logs, Metrics, Traces, and Audit Events
abstract: Kubernetes observability pipelines collect logs, metrics, traces, and audit events that are essential for reliability engineering, incident response, compliance, and capacity planning. However, these same signals frequently contain sensitive application payloads, tenant identifiers, access tokens, internal topology, operational metadata, and personally identifiable information. Conventional protections--transport encryption, storage encryption, role-based access control, and backend retention policies--do not protect telemetry while it is being parsed, enriched, sampled, correlated, redacted, routed, or queried. This creates a security gap: the observability pipeline itself becomes a privileged data-processing system. This paper proposes ConfObs-TEE, a confidential computing architecture for Kubernetes observability data. This design-science study presents a reference architecture and a prospective prototype-evaluation plan; it does not report measured implementation results. The architecture places the highest-risk telemetry operations inside hardware-backed, remotely attested Trusted Execution Environments (TEEs), while preserving compatibility with OpenTelemetry Collector patterns and Kubernetes-native deployment models. ConfObs-TEE uses attested collector agents, confidential gateway collectors, policy-bound key release, signed pipeline manifests, field-level tokenization, envelope encryption, and verifiable lineage metadata to reduce trust in cluster nodes, cloud administrators, telemetry operators, and observability backends. The design is grounded in current cloud-native mechanisms, including OpenTelemetry Collector receivers, processors, and exporters; Kubernetes metadata enrichment; Confidential Containers; Key Broker Service-style attestation; and the IETF RATS attestation model. The paper contributes a threat model for observability data in Kubernetes, a reference architecture, a policy and key-management design, a security analysis, and an evaluation methodology for future prototype validation. The central design conclusion is that confidential computing should not be applied indiscriminately to the entire observability stack, but selectively to the raw-data, enrichment, correlation, redaction, and key-handling stages where plaintext exposure and operator privilege are most consequential.

title: AVID-DR: Active-View Selection and Cross-Scale Instance-Aware Anomaly Detection with Diffusion Reconstruction
abstract: Multi-view visual analysis is often limited by redundant observations, scale-varying anomalies and incomplete image evidence. This paper proposes AVID-DR, a unified pattern-recognition framework that integrates uncertainty-guided active-view selection, confidence-weighted multi-view fusion, cross-scale instance-aware anomaly detection and structure-texture conditioned diffusion reconstruction. The key coupling is a closed uncertainty loop: detector uncertainty, reconstruction variance and fusion confidence are calibrated into a common decision signal that determines whether an additional candidate view should be processed. Candidate views are ranked using low-cost preview cues rather than full downstream inference, and the selected evidence is fused before anomaly localization and conservative reconstruction. The detector combines hierarchical features with prototype-family normal modeling, while the latent diffusion module reconstructs only anomaly-supported regions under structure and appearance constraints. Experiments use structured image degradation with document-image data as the primary empirical setting and separately evaluate localization, reconstruction and view-efficiency. The results are reported over repeated seeded runs; generalization beyond the evaluated structured-image domain is left for future study.

title: TaxoSAE: Rethinking Sparse Autoencoders through Taxonomic Logic
abstract: Recent Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) decompose the representations of large language models (LLMs) into interpretable features, enabling precise readout and control of encoded knowledge. However, existing SAEs treat each feature as a standalone unit, whereas real-world knowledge is often taxonomically organized. As a result, readout carries no guarantee of taxonomic consistency, and control lacks the granularity to specify the scope of an edit. We propose TaxoSAE, which explicitly encodes taxonomical information, built on is-a (hypernym-hyponym) relations, into the SAE feature space. TaxoSAE mirrors a taxonomy with a stack of SAEs, one per taxonomy level, and introduces a taxonomic alignment loss that trains each concept to be active whenever one of its hyponyms is. On two factual QA taxonomies, one over biographical relations and one over animals, TaxoSAE enables (1) more accurate readout through the taxonomy with concentrated activations, e.g., +31.3 points in reading out the hypernyms of abstract concepts never queried in training; (2) more precise control, with +25.5 points in swap success, while suppressing a concept removes only its own answers (0-2% accuracy vs. 91-100% on other concepts); and, more importantly, (3) readout of unseen concepts through their hypernyms, with up to +37.9 points in hypernym readout accuracy.

title: Diffusion-Based Synthesis of Complete 3D Biparametric Prostate MRI
abstract: Synthetic biparametric MRI (bpMRI) may help alleviate the limited availability of large and representative prostate MRI datasets for deep learning applications. In this work, we present a conditional 3D diffusion framework for anatomy-conditioned synthesis of complete prostate bpMRI from anatomical masks. The framework supports sequential synthesis, in which T2w and diffusion modalities are generated by separately trained models, and joint synthesis, in which all bpMRI modalities are generated simultaneously within a single model. Five configurations were trained using PI-CAI, FastMRI Prostate, and PROSTATEx datasets to investigate different conditioning schemes, target modalities, and synthesis strategies. Evaluation using distribution-based metrics, paired-image similarity, and qualitative assessment demonstrated the feasibility of both synthesis pathways. Joint synthesis achieved competitive distributional fidelity while generating complete bpMRI, whereas direct synthesis of ADC and computed high-b-value DWI outperformed their derivation from synthetic diffusion-weighted images.

title: Can Entanglement-Induced Feature-Map Designs Improve Projected Quantum Kernels?
abstract: Projected quantum kernels (PQKs) have emerged as a notable approach to circumvent the hardness of machine learning tasks arising from the exponential dimensionality of the quantum Hilbert space. However, recent PQK studies often rely heavily on extensive classical hyperparameter tuning of the radial basis function (RBF) kernel parameter and the support vector machine regularization parameter. The extensive tuning can mask the true representational power of the underlying PQKs induced by quantum feature maps, which has not been explored in detail. Thus, this work aims to expose the structural capabilities of PQKs by isolating and evaluating their native inductive bias through comparisons between untuned and tuned PQKs against the RBF baseline. Furthermore, we propose novel quantum feature maps that leverage two-qubit entanglement to capture multivariate correlations in IoT data. The results show that extensive tuning can lead to competitive performance architectures, while our proposed entanglement topologies exhibit a significantly stronger native inductive bias. This reveals that superior quantum architectural design can yield structurally better PQKs with improvements arising from quantum-mechanical properties rather than from classical hyperparameter tuning.

title: Interpretive Variation and Discourse Structure in Detecting Enthymemes in Controversial Political Discourse
abstract: Enthymemes are arguments that leave a premise or conclusion unstated, and they are a common persuasion device on social media. Because readers must fill in the missing part themselves, they often disagree on whether a text contains one. This paper asks how to detect and evaluate enthymemes when such disagreement is part of the task. On tweets about vaccination and immigration, each labeled by five annotators, F1 stalls around 0.67 for every fine-tuned model we train, regardless of data size, added features or label type. We therefore ask how these models should be evaluated instead, and propose metrics that compare predictions with the full distribution of annotator votes, together with a model that predicts this distribution directly and captures disagreement better at no cost in F1. We then ask what role discourse structure plays. Models learn to rely on explicit argumentative structure: they reliably recognize tweets without an enthymeme but rarely commit on tweets that contain one. Both the models and a discourse parser miss arguments whose links are left implicit and must be inferred by the reader. Finally, we discuss what these blind spots mean for content moderation systems trained on majority labels.

title: Relational Inference in Real-World Settings
abstract: This dissertation investigates relational inference in real-world machine learning applications across three domains: maritime security, authorship verification (AV), and kinship recognition (KR). Although these domains differ in data modality and application, they share practical challenges such as limited supervision, distribution shift, and heterogeneous, noisy data collected under uncontrolled conditions. To address these challenges, the dissertation adopts a multi-domain perspective, studying relational patterns through behavioral trajectories, textual representations, and facial imagery. The central objective is to understand how meaningful relationships can be inferred under realistic deployment constraints. Chapter 2 presents a supervised sequence learning approach for detecting maritime drug trafficking events using Automatic Identification System (AIS) vessel trajectories. A Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) network models temporal dependencies between vessels to identify coordinated "drop-off" behavior as a predictive pattern. The model achieves high recall, making it suitable for surveillance applications where early detection is essential, although precision remains limited due to the difficulty of distinguishing illicit coordination from legitimate maritime interactions. Chapter 3 addresses AV by combining RoBERTa-based semantic embeddings with handcrafted stylometric features, including sentence length, word frequency, and punctuation usage. Three neural architectures—Feature Interaction, Pairwise Concatenation, and Siamese networks—are evaluated. Incorporating stylometric information consistently improves performance, particularly recall, while the Siamese architecture achieves the strongest overall results, demonstrating the value of combining complementary semantic and stylistic representations. Chapter 4 examines model robustness under domain shift using both non-holdout settings with partial domain overlap and holdout settings containing unseen domains. While performance remains relatively stable under moderate shifts, it declines for structurally different domains such as handwritten text. Nevertheless, the proposed models consistently outperform strong PAN shared-task baselines across diverse writing domains, including essays, emails, text messages, speech-to-text transcripts, search queries, and handwritten documents. Chapter 5 explores interpretable facial representations for KR using 40 StyleGAN2-derived facial attributes. Feature-based classification models reveal that age-related characteristics and facial hair contribute most strongly to kinship predictions, whereas localized facial regions play a smaller role than expected. These findings improve understanding of which visual characteristics influence kinship recognition models. Chapter 6 evaluates deep pretrained models and supervised contrastive learning for KR by comparing KinFusionNet, a Siamese-style architecture, with the FLACL framework. Experiments using both image- and video-based inputs show that image representations consistently outperform video representations. Furthermore, models pretrained on identity-focused datasets transfer more effectively than those trained for video reconstruction, highlighting the importance of representation learning under limited supervision. Overall, the dissertation makes three main contributions. First, it demonstrates that relational inference can be successfully applied across diverse application domains by tailoring representations to behavioral, textual, and visual data. The results show that effective relational modeling depends strongly on both the type of relationship and the underlying data modality. Second, it systematically evaluates representation design across multiple architectures, including sequential modeling, combined semantic and stylometric features, and pretrained visual embeddings. The findings indicate that integrating complementary sources of information can improve robustness, provided the information contributes distinct rather than redundant signals. Third, it investigates model generalization under realistic deployment conditions through analyses of domain shift in AV and modality variation in KR. These experiments demonstrate that robustness and generalization remain the primary challenges for practical relational inference systems, with similar considerations extending to maritime surveillance applications. Across all domains, the proposed models are intended to support human decision-making rather than replace it, reflecting the ethical and practical considerations associated with deploying machine learning in real-world settings.
